title: Press Release
text:
▷ Ministry of Environment to hold ‘Water-Ojakgyo Technology Development Presentation’ linking technology needs of water companies in the field to national R&D
The Ministry of Environment (Minister Kim Wansup) announced that it will hold the ‘Water-Ojakgyo Technology Development Presentation’ on July 16 at the LW Convention Center (located in Jung-gu, Seoul), directly linking technologies needed by water companies at manufacturing sites with national R&D.
This presentation has been organized as a “platform for cooperation and communication” to enhance the effectiveness of national R&D projects in the water sector by linking them with domestic water companies.
It directly connects the technology development needs that water companies actually require in the field to national R&D projects, while presenting a new model involving the participation of water-related public institutions in the process.
Since May of this year, the Ministry has surveyed around 90 technology development needs in the water sector in collaboration with related public institutions supporting the water industry, such as the Korea Environment Corporation (Korea Water Cluster Project Group) and Korea Water Resources Corporation (K-Water).
The Korea Environmental Industry & Technology Institute (KEITI) reviewed these technology development needs for redundancy and conducted expert evaluations, ultimately selecting a total of 13 water-related technology demands earlier this month.
The 13 selected technologies are categorized as follows: two in renewable energy, six in digital water management, one in underground safety management, two in advanced analysis, and two in resource recovery.
The key contents of the representative technologies by field include: cooling technology for data centers using water thermal energy; digital water management technology utilizing artificial intelligence (AI) for coagulant dosing; safety management technology to identify water hammer points in underground pipelines; advanced analysis technology combining optical technology and AI for turbidity and bacteria detection; and wastewater resource recovery technology using biofilm reactions.
At this technology development presentation, representatives from the companies that proposed the technologies will introduce them. Following this, national R&D planning in the water sector will proceed based on final mentoring from a panel of experts comprising related institutions, academic societies, and water companies.
The Ministry plans to select these technologies as new national R&D projects as early as next year (2026) through a review process conducted by the KEITI in the second half of this year. In addition, the presentation will not be a one-time event but will be held annually on an ongoing basis.
Through this, the chronic thirst for technology development faced by water companies will be addressed, paving the way for promoting the domestic water industry and expanding the overseas presence of Korean water companies. In addition, water companies that provided the final selected technology needs will be offered incentives such as support for demonstration infrastructure, expert consulting, and participation in overseas water market development delegations as part of the Ministry’s support programs.
Kim Hyo-jung, Director General of Water Use Policy Bureau, stated, “As its name suggests, Water-Ojakgyo will serve as a bridge connecting companies and the government, the field and technology, and will become a representative case of company-centered, customized R&D.” She added, “The Ministry will continue to actively reflect technology development needs from the industrial field in policy and strive to establish a virtuous cycle where such technologies drive the industry forward.”

text:
□ The government conducted a joint special inspection with relevant ministries on July 4 to assess the impact of radioactive and heavy metal contamination on our waters and rivers in relation to concerns recently raised about wastewater from North Korea’s Pyongsan uranium concentration plant, and confirmed that there were "no abnormalities."
□ The Nuclear Safety and Security Commission, the Ministry of Oceans and Fisheries, and the Ministry of Environment collected samples from a total of 10 locations, including Ganghwa Island and the lower Han River, which are the areas closest to the estuary of the Yesong River flowing from North Korea, on July 4, and analyzed two types of radioactive nuclides including uranium, and five types of heavy metals.
□ ① Uranium: No abnormalities.
o An analysis of uranium concentrations in seawater collected from six points in the Ganghwa and Gimpo areas adjacent to the lower Yesong River (the same points as in 2019) showed levels that were either relatively lower or similar compared to 2019, when no abnormalities were observed.
o In addition, the analysis of uranium concentrations at two additional points in the estuaries of the Han River and Imjin River, as well as two points along the Incheon coast, compared to 2019 reference points (West Sea coast and Han River), also showed no significant differences.
□ ② Radioactive cesium: No abnormalities
o At all survey points, radioactive cesium was found to be below the minimum detectable activity (MDA)* or below levels measured in the West Sea over the past five years.
* The minimum detectable activity (MDA) refers to the lowest level of radioactivity that can be detected, determined by measurement conditions such as the radiation detector, sample volume, recovery rate, and measurement time.
□ ③ Heavy metals (5 types): No abnormalities
o At all points, the levels of heavy metals were either below the standards or not detected, based on the environmental standards under the Framework Act on Environmental Policy and the marine environmental standards under the Act on the Conservation and Utilization of the Marine Environment.
* According to the "Official Test Standards for Water Pollution," if the measured concentration is below the quantification limit, it is recorded as "Not detected."
□ The government plans to maintain a monthly monitoring system for the seven key points covered in the recent survey and continue operating the inter-agency consultative body, thereby actively responding to public concerns at a whole-of-government level.

text:
▷ Selected: Gangwon Peace Area, Gangwon Paleozoic, Busan, Hantangang River, Jinan/Muju, and Uiseong
The National Geopark Office* of the Korea National Park Service (KNPS, Chairman Joo Dae-young) under the Ministry of Environment recommended “Earth Exploration 6 Geoparks” that families can enjoy together during summer vacation.
* Pursuant to Article 80 of the Natural Parks Act (Delegation and Entrustment of Authority) and Article 45 of its Enforcement Decree, matters related to the management and operation of geoparks, support, and the selection and utilization of geopark interpreters are entrusted to the Korea National Park Service.
A national geopark is a geopark certified by the state as geologically significant and having outstanding landscapes. It shall be conserved and can be used for education and tourism. A global geopark is designated through deliberation by the UNESCO Global Geoparks Council.
The six geoparks recommended this time by the KNPS are Gangwon Peace Area, Gangwon Paleozoic, Busan, Hantangang River, Jinan-Muju, and Uiseong.
The Gangwon Peace Area National Geopark is located in Yanggu County, featuring Dutayeon Valley and the Yanggu Porcelain Museum as key attractions. Dutayeon showcases river erosion that forms deep valleys, and its cascading waterfall resembles the outline of the Korean Peninsula. Entry requires a reservation through the Yanggu Security Tourism website (stour.ticketplay.zone) or on-site at the Dutayeon Geumgangsan Road Information Center, and visitors must present ID. At the Yanggu Porcelain Museum (closed every Monday), visitors can experience making white porcelain using a pottery wheel. Yanggu’s white clay has been renowned for its quality since the late Goryeo period, offering ideal conditions for pottery making.
The Gangwon Paleozoic National Geopark is located in Pyeongchang County, with Baengnyong Cave, a limestone cave, as its representative geological attraction. It is the only “exploration-type cave” in Korea.
Maintaining a constant temperature of 13°C and about 90% humidity year-round, it is home to various species such as cave beetles, bats, and fungi, making it a key site for environmental education. Starting in July, geological tours such as the “Gangwon Paleozoic Geopark Grand Exploration” and “Planet Pyeongchang” will be offered with local experts, covering geological sites around Pyeongchang and Jeongseon. Reservations can be made through the related website (Bold Trip, boldtrip.co.kr).
At the Busan National Geopark, visitors can enjoy the refreshing sea breeze at Taejongdae Park and join the “Earth Time Travel!” guided program led by a geopark interpreter at the Taejongdae Information Center. Those who make a reservation in advance through the Busan National Geopark website (http://www.busan.go.kr/geopark) will also receive a souvenir.
The Hantangang River Geopark features standout programs such as the “Hantangang River Geo-Touring” and “Summer Weekend Activities.” The Geo-Touring program, held on weekends from July 12 to August 24, includes visits to Hwajeogyeon Pool, Meonguri Gorge, and Bidulginang Falls with a geopark interpreter. At the Hantangang River Global Geopark Center in Pocheon City, geology-themed educational activities, such as making bracelets with basalt, are offered every weekend from July through August.
At the Jinan-Muju National Geopark, visitors can cool off from the heat with water activities at Unilam Banilam. This valley, known for its striking rock formations created by volcanic activity during the Cretaceous period of the Mesozoic era, is a popular summer destination. The “Water Playground Under the Clouds,” which opened on July 18, offers a safe space for water play, and visitors can also escape the heat by walking across the thrilling suspension bridge over Unilam Banilam.
The Uiseong Geopark features Binggye Valley in Binggye-ri, Chunsan-myeon, as its representative geological attraction-a natural air-conditioning site. Formed by volcanic activity at the end of the Cretaceous period in the Mesozoic era, the area consists of basalt and tuff. It has ice caves where ice does not melt even in summer, and wind holes where compressed air escapes through gaps in the rocks beneath piles of stones in the valley. A visit to Binggye Valley offers a refreshing and pleasant retreat in nature, even in the peak of summer.
Kwon Eun-jung, Director of the National Geopark Office at the KNPS, stated, “We hope families will visit geoparks during summer vacation to enjoy various hands-on geological education experiences and have a refreshing summer holiday.”

text:
▷ Administrative notice of the revised ‘Notice on the Designation of Circular Resources’ (July 21-August 11)
▷ Waste regulations exempted when usage, methods, and standards for newly designated circular items are followed
The Ministry of Environment announced that, in order to promote the circular use of waste resources, it will issue a 20-day administrative notice starting July 21 on a revised bill to designate the three additional items of “waste cooking oil,” “coffee grounds,” and “rice husks and bran” as circular resources.
The term “circular resources” refers to substances or objects among waste that, under the Act on Promotion of Transition to Circular Economy and Society, are not harmful to human health or the environment, have economic value and can be traded for payment, and are not likely to be abandoned. Once designated and announced as circular resources, they are exempt from waste regulations without a separate application if they comply with the specified usage, methods, and standards for circular resources. Currently, seven items, including waste paper, are designated and managed as such.
* (Items) ① Waste paper, ② Scrap iron, ③ Waste metal cans, ④ Aluminum, ⑤ Copper, ⑥ Waste batteries from electric vehicles, ⑦ Waste glass
Starting in April this year (2025), the Ministry of Environment established a consultative body consisting of relevant organizations, companies, and experts to cover the entire process from waste generation to collection, transport, and recycling. Through gathering stakeholder opinions, it prepared the announcement to designate waste cooking oil and the other two items as circular resources.
First, “waste cooking oil” is seeing a surge in demand as a raw material for petroleum alternative fuels such as Sustainable Aviation Fuels (SAF), so it is expected to be more easily recycled once designated as a circular resource.
“Coffee grounds” are also continuously increasing in volume due to rising coffee consumption in Korea. Once designated as a circular resource, they are expected to be reused in various fields such as compost, construction materials, and household goods.
“Rice husks and bran” are by-products generated during rice milling and are already actively recycled as livestock bedding, feed, or compost, making them highly safe and suitable for circular use. The three newly added circular items will be exempt from waste-related regulations under the Waste Control Act, including industrial waste discharger reporting, collection and transport permits, waste storage periods, and waste treatment business permits, if they comply with the designated usage, methods, and standards for circular resources.
Details of the revised notice, including the usage and standards for circular use, can be found on the National Legislative Participation Center (opinion.lawmaking.go.kr) and the Ministry of Environment’s website (http://www.me.go.kr).
To promote proper use and understanding of the newly added circular resources, the Ministry of Environment will distribute a guidebook on the certification and designation/notification system for circular resources to local governments nationwide within this month. The ministry also plans to hold regional on-site briefings* for organizations and companies handling the newly designated items.
* Explanation of the circular resource certification and designation/notification system, guidance on the item-specific information registration procedures, etc.
Kim Go-eung, Director General of the Resources Circulation Bureau at the Ministry of Environment, stated, “The circular use of these three items, which have high demand for circular resource utilization, is expected to become more active.” He added, “We will continue to engage with the industry to secure domestic supply chains for key circular resources and promote their circular use.”
For further information, please contact the Public Relations Division.

text:
▷ Ministry of Environment and Korea Environment Institute to hold international symposium on climate adaptation
The Ministry of Environment and the Korea Environment Institute announced that they will hold the “2025 International Symposium on Climate Change Adaptation” on the theme of “Enhancing the Effectiveness of National Climate Change Adaptation Policy” on July 23 at the Korea Chamber of Commerce and Industry in Jung-gu, Seoul.
Recently, abnormal climate events caused by the climate crisis have continued across the globe, highlighting the growing importance of climate change adaptation policies. In particular, at the 29th Conference of the Parties (COP29) to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change held in Azerbaijan in November 2024, the Global Goal on Adaptation (GGA)* was established as a standing agenda item, and the “Baku Adaptation Roadmap” was adopted, signaling the full-scale launch of international discussions on climate adaptation.
* ① Enhanced Adaptive Capacity, ② Strengthened Resilience, ③ Reduced Vulnerability
Since 2010, Korea has designated the Korea Adaptation Center for Climate Change (KACCC) and has been implementing systematic climate adaptation policies by establishing national adaptative measures for climate crisis” every five years. Internationally, Korea has also demonstrated its role as a leading country in climate adaptation by consistently operating the “Climate Adaptation Global Academy” training program since 2009 to provide capacity-building education on climate adaptation to neighboring countries.
This symposium has been organized in this context to share Korea’s exemplary climate adaptation policy cases and to explore strategies for international cooperation in the field of climate adaptation.
The event will be attended by domestic and international experts, including Sandro Demaio, Director of the WHO Asia-Pacific Centre for Environment and Health, Professor Kim Hyung-jun of KAIST, as well as representatives responsible for climate adaptation from the UNFCCC, the European Union (EU), Japan, and China.
The symposium will consist of two sessions. The first session, under the theme “Evaluation Methods for Advancing Adaptation Policies,” will include presentations and a comprehensive discussion on the following topics: 1) a comprehensive strategic framework for responding to the climate crisis, 2) Korea’s evaluation system for climate crisis adaptation plans, and 3) the current status of discussions on developing indicators for the GGA (including cases from Germany and the European Union).
The second session, under the theme “Strengthening Adaptation Strategies Through Community Participation,” will feature presentations and a comprehensive discussion on regional cooperation cases in the Asia-Pacific region (including Korea, Japan, and China), and capacity building for local climate adaptation.
Vice Minister of Environment Kum Hanseung stated, “We are all experiencing the escalating climate crisis firsthand, with record-breaking heatwaves and heavy rains.” He added, “Through this international symposium, we will promote scientific and systematic climate adaptation policies and work closely with the international community to advance global climate adaptation.”

▷ Full-scale production of green hydrogen for vehicles begins at Seongnam Water Purification Plant’s water electrolysis hydrogen production facility
▷ Supplying up to 188kg per day of green hydrogen to hydrogen refueling stations, enough to fuel 38 hydrogen passenger vehicles
The Ministry of Environment (Minister Kim Sungwhan) and the K-Water (CEO Yun Seog-dae) announced that they will hold a commemorative event for the shipment of green hydrogen at the Seongnam Water Purification Plant (Seongnam-si, Gyeonggi-do) on the morning of July 23, together with organizations including the Korea Automobile Environment Association and the Korea Hydrogen Environment Association, and will begin full-scale supply to hydrogen refueling stations.
Supplying green hydrogen to hydrogen refueling stations represents the nation’s first case of providing carbon-free clean energy produced by electrolyzing water with electricity generated from eco-friendly renewable hydropower.
The green hydrogen production facility at the Seongnam Water Purification Plant was constructed as part of a project initiated in 2022 to establish a foundation for expanding hydrogen vehicle adoption toward achieving “2050 Carbon Neutrality,” with a total investment of KRW 4.4 billion (KRW 3.1 billion from government funding and KRW 1.3 billion from K-Water).
The facility can produce up to 188kg of green hydrogen per day (enough to fuel about 38 hydrogen passenger vehicles), or up to 62 tons annually. Until September of this year, hydrogen will be transported by vehicle to the Seongnam Hydrogen Refueling Station (546-7 Galhyeon-dong, Jungwon-gu, Seongnam-si). From October onward, it will be directly supplied via pipeline to a hydrogen refueling station installed near the Seongnam Water Purification Plant.
Meanwhile, the Ministry of Environment, in collaboration with Miryang City and Chungju City, is constructing green hydrogen production facilities at Miryang Dam and Chungju Dam* using hydropower energy. Upon completion in 2028, these facilities will additionally produce 1,069 kg of green hydrogen daily, enough to refuel approximately 214 hydrogen passenger vehicles.
* Miryang Dam (2023-2026): Daily maximum production of 429 kg; Chungju Dam (2023-2027): Daily maximum production of 640 kg
Moving forward, close cooperation with local governments will continue to expand projects for green hydrogen production facilities using renewable energy. This aims to establish a regionally self-sufficient hydrogen production system, producing hydrogen locally for local use, thereby ensuring a stable hydrogen supply, improving economic efficiency of supply pricing, and enhancing convenience for vehicle refueling.
Ryu Pil-mu, Director of the Air Quality Future Strategy Division at the Ministry of Environment, stated, “The supply of green hydrogen to hydrogen refueling stations signifies the transition of green hydrogen, a clean energy source in the era of climate crisis, from the demonstration stage to full-scale utilization.” He added, “We will continue establishing a stable supply chain for green hydrogen for vehicle use, contributing not only to expanding the distribution of hydrogen vehicles but also to revitalizing the domestic hydrogen economy.”

text:
▷ “Protecting Wetlands for Our Common Future” to be discussed in Zimbabwe from July 23 to 31
▷ New strategic plan outlining Ramsar Convention goals through 2034 to be adopted
The Ministry of Environment announced that the 15th meeting of the Conference of the Contracting Parties to the Ramsar Convention on Wetlands (Ramsar COP15)* will be held from July 24 to 31 in Victoria Falls, Zimbabwe.
* The Ramsar Convention is an international environmental treaty adopted in 1971 to prevent the loss and degradation of wetlands, which hold high ecological, social, economic, and cultural value. South Korea joined the convention in 1997 and hosted the 10th meeting of the Conference of the Contracting Parties in Changwon in 2008.
The Ramsar COP15 will be attended by representatives from 172 member countries and experts from international organizations. South Korea will be represented by a government delegation composed of officials from the Ministry of Environment and other relevant agencies, as well as experts.
The upcoming Ramsar COP15 will be held under the theme “Protecting Wetlands for Our Common Future,” highlighting the vital role of wetlands in addressing the three major environmental crises: biodiversity loss, pollution, and climate change. The conference will seek to build global solidarity to prevent the loss of wetlands and ensure their protection.
On July 24, the host country Zimbabwe will hold a high-level discussion on topics such as international cooperation for wetland conservation and strengthening local livelihoods through wetland preservation. The goal is to unite the commitment of the contracting parties and adopt the “Victoria Declaration.”
The conference will also include the presentation of reports from the Ramsar Convention Secretariat on the implementation status of the convention. Key agenda items include discussions on the “Ramsar Strategic Plan 2025-2034,” the convention’s mid- to long-term roadmap, as well as draft resolutions proposed by member countries for wetland protection.
The “Ramsar Strategic Plan 2025-2034” outlines specific implementation goals for the convention through 2034. Based on this plan, member countries will be required to submit national reports detailing their implementation progress. As a result, intense negotiations are expected among the parties, particularly on contentious issues such as mobilizing financial resources for developing countries.
A key agenda item at this conference will be the draft resolution on “Vulnerability Assessment of Wetlands,” led and proposed by South Korea. The resolution emphasizes the need to assess the vulnerability of wetlands to factors that negatively impact their ecological characteristics, such as climate change. It calls on contracting parties to incorporate assessments of ecological vulnerability into their wetland monitoring efforts.
During the conference, a key event will be the certification ceremony for newly designated Wetland Cities, scheduled for July 24 from 3:00 to 4:00 p.m. local time. This year, South Korea’s cities of Mungyeong and Gimhae have been newly designated and will receive official certification. In connection with this, the Wetland City Forum will be held to introduce the new Wetland Cities and share experiences from existing ones. The forum will take place in two parts: Part 1 on July 24 from 4:00 to 5:00 p.m., and Part 2 on July 25 from 3:00 to 6:00 p.m. local time.
※ The Wetland City Accreditation system was established through a resolution proposed by South Korea and Tunisia, which was adopted at the Ramsar COP12 in 2015 to strengthen wetland conservation at the local community level. This year, 31 new Wetland Cities and 18 re-accredited cities have been designated, bringing the total to 74 Wetland Cities across 27 countries.
Jung Eun-hae, Director General for International Cooperation Bureau at the Ministry of Environment, stated, “In this era of climate crisis, the importance of wetlands as carbon sinks will be highlighted once again.” She added, “Through this conference, we will work to more closely align South Korea’s wetland conservation policies with the international community.”

title: Press Release
text:
▷ Minister Kim Sungwhan visits Hyundai Motor Company Jeonju plant to discuss promotion of domestically produced electric commercial vehicles
▷ Inspection of electric commercial vehicle production and distribution status and hearing from manufacturers
The Ministry of Environment (Minister Kim Sungwhan) announced that on
the afternoon of July 24, Minister Kim Sungwhan would visit Hyundai Motor Company Jeonju plant (located in Wanju-gun, Jeollabuk-do) to inspect the production and distribution site of electric commercial vehicles and discuss ways to promote the distribution of domestically produced electric commercial vehicles with officials.
Since beginning vehicle production in 1995, Hyundai Motor Company Jeonju plant launched its first electric bus (Elec City) in 2017. In May of last year (2024), it upgraded its production line to increase the annual planned production of electric buses by approximately 2.5 times (from 1,450 to 3,600 units), thereby strengthening its electric commercial vehicle production capacity. As the world’s largest electric commercial vehicle plant in a single location, it produces a total of 17 types of commercial vehicles, including electric and internal combustion buses and trucks.
This site visit was arranged to both commend the efforts of on-site personnel and to listen to firsthand opinions on the challenges and efforts required to achieve the goal of distributing 4.5 million electric and hydrogen vehicles by 2030 without delay. It also aimed to discuss obstacles to the distribution of domestically produced electric commercial vehicles and ways to overcome them.
As of the cumulative total in June 2025, approximately 845,000 electric and hydrogen vehicles have been distributed. While the demand for electric vehicles had somewhat slowed after 2023, it has shown signs of recovery this year*. Electric and hydrogen buses, which have significant environmental benefits, continue to grow steadily without a decline in demand**. Among the 12,830 electric buses distributed domestically from 2011 to June 2025, 59.6% were domestically produced and 40.4% were imported.
* As of June 2025, approximately 95,000 electric and hydrogen vehicles have been distributed, marking an increase of about 44% compared to the same period in 2024 (66,000 vehicles).
** (Electric Buses) (2022) 2,074 units → (2023) 2,820 units → (2024) 3,611 units → (June 2025) 1,179 units
(Hydrogen Buses) (2022) 152 units → (2023) 368 units → (2024) 1,044 units → (June 2025) 524 units
Minister Kim Sungwhan stated, “The electric vehicle industry is not only a next-generation growth engine that will drive the national economy, but also a key force in achieving carbon neutrality in the transportation sector.” He added, “We will actively promote the distribution of domestically produced electric commercial vehicles by enhancing the efficiency of subsidy policies to strengthen the competitiveness of the domestic electric commercial vehicle industry.”

title: Press Release

▷ Ministry of Environment, Air Force, and Korea Resource Circulation Service Agency sign agreement to boost resource recycling in military bases
The Ministry of Environment (Minister Kim Sunghwan) announced that it will sign a business agreement on July 29 at the Air Force Headquarters (located in Gyeryong-si, Chungcheongnam-do) with the Air Force (Chief of Staff Lee Young-su) and the Korea Resource Circulation Service Agency (KORA, Chairman Lee Myung-hwan) to promote resource recycling.
Military bases, where large-scale personnel and resources are concentrated, are required to play a leading role in waste management, and cooperation in recycling within the military is essential to address plastic pollution and transition to a circular economy.
The Air Force has also expressed a strong willingness to actively participate in promoting recycling and has decided to cooperate with the Ministry of Environment, taking into account the entire resource recycling cycle from the separation of recyclable materials to the use of recycled products.
The agreement specifically includes: support for dedicated collection facilities for paper packs and transparent PET bottles at Air Force units; use of recycled products produced through the Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) system; resource recycling education for service members; and evaluation and reward support for outstanding units.
Kim Go-eung, Director General of the Resource Circulation Bureau at the Ministry of Environment, stated, “The cooperation of approximately 65,000 Air Force personnel is expected to play a role in ensuring a stable supply of recycled materials and driving demand in the recycling market.” He added, “We will actively support the creation of a circular economy ecosystem within military bases.”
Park Geun-woo, Chief of the Air Force Engineering Office, stated, "This is significant in strengthening environmental management at the military level and creating a sustainable defense environment." He also emphasized, “We will do our best to raise awareness of resource recycling among service members and achieve tangible recycling outcomes.”

text:
▷ Reviewing national greenhouse gas reduction strategies and discussing key takeaways
The Greenhouse Gas Inventory and Research Center of Korea (President Choi Min-ji), under the Ministry of Environment, will hold the 16th International Greenhouse Gas Conference on Friday, August 1, at the EL Tower in Yangjae, Seocho-gu, Seoul.
At this conference, strategies for implementing the Paris Agreement goals will be shared through case presentations from various countries, including Singapore, Japan, the United Kingdom, Germany, and the European Union (EU).
Presenters of international case studies include: Rene Freitag, Chief Advisor at the Deutsche Gesellschaft fur Internationale Zusammenarbeit (GIZ); Kevin Ong, First Secretary at the Embassy of Singapore in Korea; Mikiko Kainuma, Senior Research Advisor at the Institute for Global Environmental Strategies (IGES) in Japan; Jonathan Woodland, Head of Climate, Energy & Enablers, Economic Diplomacy Team at the British Embassy in Korea; and Jonghan Lee, Environment and Climate Policy Officer at the Delegation of the European Union to Korea. On the Korean side, Hyungkwan Ryu, Director of the Climate Change Strategy Division at the Ministry of Environment, will present on behalf of the Korean government.
In the following discussion session, Professor Seungjick Yoo of Sookmyung Women’s University will serve as moderator. The panel will include Youngjoon Cho, Executive Director of Sustainable Management Institution at the Korea Chamber of Commerce and Industry; Sangjae Ryu, Co-Representative of the Korean Youth Climate Change Network BigWave; and Yoon Sowon, Researcher at the Greenhouse Gas Inventory and Research Center. They will review the greenhouse gas reduction levels and implementation strategies of various countries and discuss the implications.
Prior to the main event, a side event will be held in the morning under the theme “Lessons from the First Biennial Transparency Report (BTR),” where government experts from six countries, namely, Rwanda, Zimbabwe, the Philippines, Turkiye, Sri Lanka, and Argentina, will share their experiences and challenges in preparing their BTRs and discuss the technical and institutional support needed for implementing transparency frameworks.
This side event was organized as part of the “2025 International Greenhouse Gas Experts Training,” which has been underway since July 14 at Sejong University, hosted by the Greenhouse Gas Inventory and Research Center and the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) Secretariat.
Choi Min-ji, President of the Greenhouse Gas Inventory and Research Center, stated, “The 2035 Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC) is not just about setting a target; it’s about designing policies with real implementability.” She added, “We hope this conference serves as an opportunity for countries to take a more proactive approach to the climate crisis and seek practical solutions.”

▷ Discussions on artificial intelligence flood forecasting, smart leak management, and expanding renewable energy cooperation
▷ Promotion of a five-year joint cooperation plan to tackle the climate crisis between the two countries
The Ministry of Environment (Minister Kim Sungwhan) announced that it will hold the 3rd Korea-Thailand Water Management Cooperation Joint Committee meeting at the Sejong Government Complex on August 5.
The Korea-Thailand Water Management Cooperation Joint Committee (the Joint Committee) is being promoted as a follow-up to the Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) on water management signed in Bangkok in September 2019 in the presence of the leaders of both countries. The 1st Joint Committee was held in October 2019, and the 2nd in August 2021. It has been resumed on the occasion of the 3rd Mekong-Korea International Water Forum held in March this year.
At this 3rd Joint Committee, Kim Hyo-jung, Director General of the Water Use Policy Bureau at the Ministry of Environment, along with domestic water management experts, will attend as the Korean delegation. Representing Thailand, Surasri Kidtimonton, Secretary-General of the Office of the National Water Resources, and 11 others including officials from Nakhon Ratchasima City, will participate.
In 2023, Thailand experienced a 28% decrease in rainfall compared to 2022 due to the impact of El Nino, and last year, the water level of the Chiang Mai River reached an all-time high as typhoons coincided with the rainy season, creating a situation that necessitates the establishment of water management measures in response to the climate crisis.
In addition, Thailand is promoting the digital and artificial intelligence (AI) sectors as new growth engines and is interested in digital water management to enhance climate resilience. Accordingly, there is growing interest in areas where Korean water companies have strengths, such as real-time water management monitoring, data management, and predictive analytics.
The Joint Committee will focus on three main areas for policy and technology exchange between the two countries: enhancing water disaster response capabilities using an AI-based flood forecasting system, smart leak reduction technology, and establishment and management of renewable energy systems in the water sector.
In addition, the two countries will share their water management policies and technological needs and discuss establishing a five-year cooperation plan to address the shared challenge of the climate crisis.
After the Joint Committee meeting, the Thai delegation will visit the Jungnang Sewage Treatment Center, Korea’s first modern sewage treatment plant, which increases energy self-sufficiency by utilizing biogas extracted during the treatment process, and the Seongnam Water Purification Plant, which produces green hydrogen using a micro-hydropower-based electrolysis method.
Director General Kim Hyo-jung stated, “This Joint Committee is an opportunity to share Korea’s strengths in AI-based flood forecasting, smart water network management technology, and advanced sewage treatment technologies.” He added, “We plan to identify and promote customized cooperation projects that help solve local water issues in Thailand while facilitating the overseas expansion of Korean water companies.”

▷ Review of subsidy execution status including local government funding for EV subsidies, and hearing difficulties from subsidy implementers
▷ Request for continued support from central and local governments to build a sustainable domestic EV ecosystem
The Ministry of Environment (Minister Kim Sungwhan) announced that on the afternoon of August 6, Vice Minister Kum Hanseung will hold an inspection meeting at the Ministry’s conference room in the Government Complex Sejong with local governments (17 cities and provinces) and the Korea Environment Corporation to review the execution status of electric vehicle (EV) subsidies and discuss improvement measures for the smooth implementation of the 2025 EV supply project.
The domestic EV market experienced a temporary stagnation in demand (EV chasm) and incidents of fires in 2023-2024, leading to a slowdown. However, signs of recovery and expanded adoption are emerging in 2025. Accordingly, this meeting was organized to ensure the smooth execution of EV subsidies, secure momentum for the transition to EVs, and further accelerate the trend of widespread adoption.
* As of July 2024, 80,620 units were registered → approximately a 47% increase compared to the same period last year.
This meeting will discuss issues raised during the implementation of the EV supply project, including: execution status by local governments; insufficient local budget allocation and regional disparities in subsidy distribution; plans for early execution of electric bus subsidies; and issues related to local government settlements. In addition, discussions will be held on cooperation measures between the central and local governments for the smooth implementation of the remaining 2025 supply project, along with hearing difficulties encountered during subsidy execution.
Based on the results of this meeting, the Ministry plans to reallocate subsidies by local government and vehicle type, prioritizing regions with concentrated demand, and to reflect improvements in the revised subsidy guidelines for the following year. In addition, local governments will consider additional local budget allocations to ensure more EV consumers can benefit from the subsidies.
Vice Minister Kum stated, “Support policies, including subsidies, are extremely important for achieving carbon neutrality and building a sustainable domestic EV industry ecosystem.” He added, “The government and local governments will work together to improve subsidy execution and smoothly implement the 2025 EV supply project, thereby securing momentum and accelerating the adoption of EVs in Korea.”

▷ Support for overseas expansion and order acquisition of domestic companies in the water and renewable energy sectors
The Ministry of Environment (Minister Kim Sungwhan) announced that it will dispatch a “Green Industry Support Task Force” to Jakarta, Indonesia, from August 11 to 14.
This dispatch is being carried out to resolve difficulties faced by domestic companies in ongoing order projects in Indonesia and to strengthen networks with clients, focusing on the water industry, which has promising prospects for future overseas expansion.
The Task Force plans to promote overseas expansion in areas such as water supply and sewage, hydropower, and carbon reduction through: intergovernmental environmental cooperation meetings with Indonesian government agencies (such as the Ministry of Public Works and Public Housing, the Ministry of Environment, and the Ministry of Energy and Mineral Resources), the Korea-Indonesia Water Cooperation Seminar, and one-on-one export and order consultations between domestic water companies and Indonesian clients.
On the first day (August 12), the “Korea-Indonesia Water Cooperation Seminar” will share information on Indonesia’s water industry policy direction, the current status of digital transformation in the water sector, and issues and countermeasures related to regional Non-Revenue Water* (NRW) generation. Following this, 12 domestic companies will present new technologies and products related to improving water revenue rates, pipeline network management, seawater desalination, and water treatment plants. After the seminar, in-depth consultations between local clients and domestic companies will be held through one-on-one meetings with the clients.
* The amount of tap water produced in the water supply process that is not monetized through billing.
On the second day (August 13), intergovernmental cooperation meetings with Indonesia’s Ministry of Energy and Mineral Resources and Ministry of Environment will discuss the issue of recognizing carbon credits for renewable energy projects, such as the Siborpa Hydropower Project (114 MW) being promoted by Korea Midland Power and the Hasang Hydropower Project (41 MW) being promoted by LX International. Although the Indonesian government announced in March this year that it would recognize carbon credits for private companies (including foreign companies), actual recognition has been delayed due to shortcomings in the relevant local systems.
Through these discussions, the Ministry plans to request cooperation from the Indonesian government (Ministry of Energy and Mineral Resources and Ministry of Environment) to ensure the prompt recognition of carbon credits for private companies. If carbon credits for renewable energy projects carried out by private companies, including foreign companies, are recognized in the future, the entry of domestic companies into Indonesia’s renewable energy market is expected to expand significantly.
Jung Eun-hae, Director General of the International Cooperation Bureau at the Ministry of Environment, stated, “The green partnership with Indonesia will expand overseas order opportunities for domestic companies and create both economic and environmental value.” She added, “We will closely examine on-site difficulties and provide support to ensure they lead to tangible contracts and investments.”

title: Press Release

▷ MOU and academic symposium for ecosystem preservation and Dokdo ecology to commemorate the 80th anniversary of liberation, expanding social value management activities through public-private cooperation
The National Institute of Ecology (NIE, Director Lee Chang-suk), under the Ministry of Environment, announced that it signed a memorandum of understanding (MOU) with Naver (CEO Choi Soo-yeon) on August 13 at Naver’s headquarters in Bundang-gu, Seongnam, for the conservation of ecosystems and related matters, and that it would hold a joint academic symposium for the preservation of Dokdo’s outstanding natural ecosystem.
Through this agreement, the two institutions will strengthen cooperation in various areas such as a task force on nature-related financial disclosure (TNFD), biodiversity, and ecology-related events and academic forums, and plan to work closely so that the private and public sectors can actively carry out social value management (ESG) activities.
This MOU was established to combine the NIE's ecological research data with Naver’s digital platform capabilities, in order to provide trusted ecological and environmental information to society as a whole.
Following the signing of the MOU on that day, a joint academic forum will be held to commemorate the 80th anniversary of liberation, under the theme ‘Dokdo’s Ecology Symposium-Dokdo’s Ecology Resembles the East Sea Coast of the Korean Peninsula.‘
At this event, there will be presentations and discussions on a variety of topics, including Dokdo’s ecosystem biodiversity, Dokdo’s ecological value and significance, the direction of mid- to long-term ecological research policy, and Naver’s environmentally friendly efforts.
In particular, the NIE will share the results of years of accumulated detailed ecological surveys of Dokdo and the status of conservation policy implementation, and Naver will introduce its efforts toward eco-friendliness and biodiversity.
The NIE will continue to pursue science-based policy development for the conservation and use of key national ecological resources, including Dokdo, and, as a result of this cooperation, plans to take the lead in building a digital-based natural capital system.
Director Lee Chang-suk of the NIE said, “Public-private cooperation is more important now than ever.” He added, “With this agreement and the academic symposium as an opportunity, we will strengthen Koreaa’s ecological sovereignty and take the first step toward cooperation for ecosystem conservation and sustainable management.”

text:
▷ Negotiations to Continue Through Follow-up Meetings
The Second Part of the Fifth Session of the Intergovernmental Negotiating Committee (INC*-5.2) for drafting a global treaty on plastic pollution, held in Geneva, Switzerland from August 5 (Tue) to August 15 (Fri), concluded without reaching an agreement on the treaty text despite intense discussions until the final day. The meeting was originally scheduled to end on August 14 (Thu), but negotiations continued until the deadline was exceeded, finally ending at 9 a.m. on August 15 (Fri).
※ Background of the treaty initiative: In February 2022, at the 5th United Nations Environment Assembly (UNEA), a resolution was adopted to pursue the drafting of a global treaty. Through the Intergovernmental Negotiating Committee (INC) meetings, the goal was set to develop a legally binding treaty text.
* Intergovernmental Negotiating Committee to develop an international legally binding instrument on plastic pollution, including in the marine environment
At this Intergovernmental Negotiating Committee meeting, more than 3,700 participants attended, including government delegations from over 180 UN member states, as well as stakeholders from international organizations, industry, civil society, and academia. From Korea, the government delegation was composed of officials from the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, the Ministry of Environment, the Ministry of Trade, Industry and Energy, and the Ministry of Oceans and Fisheries.
※ Chief Representative: Chung Kee-yong, Ambassador and Deputy Minister for Climate Change, Ministry of Foreign Affairs.
This second part of the fifth session was convened as a follow-up after the INC-5.1 session, held in Busan, South Korea, in November 2024, failed to produce a treaty draft due to sharp disagreements among countries over key issues. Member states began discussions based on the Chair’s draft text reflecting the outcomes of INC-5.1, but made no progress as positions remained deeply divided on major issues such as whether to regulate plastic production, the scope and methods of regulating plastic products, and the mechanisms for financing and support. Member states agreed to continue negotiations by holding further additional sessions based on the results of the discussions so far.
As the host country of INC-5.1, the Korean delegation continued to play a constructive role in seeking treaty conclusion by actively presenting compromise proposals to narrow the differing positions among parties. In particular, the delegation facilitated small-group discussions by bringing together countries with diverse views on key provisions such as product regulation and product design. It also submitted a policy report aimed at fostering common understanding on measures to strengthen product circularity, thereby working to build a constructive foundation for negotiations.
In addition, Chief Representative Chung Kee-yong, Ambassador for Climate Change, worked toward reaching a treaty through bilateral consultations with the chief representatives of the United States, Turkiye, the EU, Japan, Switzerland, and others. Furthermore, on August 12 (Tue)-13 (Wed), Ambassador Chung attended the high-level roundtable hosted by UNEP, where he introduced the Korean government’s various efforts to advance the transition to a circular economy. On August 12 (Tue), he also held a meeting with environmental civic groups to exchange views on the status and prospects of the negotiations.
Ambassador Chung stated, “Despite the intense negotiations held during this additional session following three years of prior discussions, we were unable to conclude an agreement to address the plastic issue. However, I believe this reflects both the differing interests of countries in tackling plastic pollution while protecting their economic benefits, and the high level of international attention on resolving this matter. As the host country of INC-5.1 in Busan last year, Korea will continue to play a bridging role in the upcoming negotiations to help foster compromise among countries with differing positions.”
The Korean government will continue to actively contribute to the establishment of international norms in the environmental field in order to lead the way in ending plastic pollution and advancing the transition to a circular economy.

text:
▷ Ministry of Environment to host 2025 UNFCCC-CASTT Adaptation Academy in Asia and the Pacific in Jeju
The Ministry of Environment (Minister Kim Sungwhan) and the Korea Environment Institute (KEI, President Kim Hongkyun) announced that they will hold the ‘2025 UNFCCC-CASTT Adaptation Academy in Asia and the Pacific’ for five days starting August 25 at the United Nations Institute for Training and Research (UNITAR) Jeju International Training Center (JITC), located in Seogwipo, Jeju.
This event is hosted by the Ministry of Environment and co-organized by the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) Secretariat, KEI, JITC, and United Nations Environment Program (UNEP) Copenhagen Climate Centre. It will target officials* in charge of climate adaptation in the Asia-Pacific region, introducing Korea’s climate adaptation policy cases and providing practical training on preparing national climate adaptation reports (Biennial Transparency Reports submitted to the UN).
* A total of 20 officials from 12 countries, including Mongolia, Bangladesh, and the Philippines.
Since 2009, Korea has been providing climate adaptation capacity-building training for neighboring countries, and since 2021, it has linked this program with the UNFCCC programme*, continuously contributing to strengthening climate adaptation capacity in the international community.
* UNFCCC Climate Action and Support Transparency Training (UNFCCC-CASTT) Programme
In particular, this year marks the first time that the adaptation academy, which had previously been conducted only overseas and online, is being hosted domestically, thereby laying the foundation for expanding international cooperation in the field of climate adaptation.
The theme of this event is “Climate Transparency and Adaptation Action: Building capacity on adaptation reporting through BTR1 Experiences.” Through this, officials from each participating country will focus on strengthening their capabilities in formulating climate adaptation policies and preparing national reports.
Under the Paris Agreement* of the UNFCCC, all Parties are required to submit a Biennial Transparency Report (BTR) every two years starting in 2024, transparently reporting their progress in responding to climate change. In addition, based on the Paris Agreement, the UNFCCC Secretariat recommends that each Party also submit an adaptation report.
* The international agreement adopted at the 21st Conference of the Parties (COP21) to the UNFCCC on December 12, 2015.
Since 2010, Korea has been formulating and implementing the ‘National Climate Crisis Adaptation Plan’ every five years, and has submitted both the Korea Climate Change Adaptation Report and the First BTR to the UNFCCC Secretariat. Through this event, Korea will share its experience in establishing climate adaptation policies and reporting with officials from various countries, and, together with international organizations, will carry out practical training on report preparation.
Ahn Se-chang, Deputy Minister of Climate Change and Carbon Neutral Policy Office at the Ministry of Environment, stated, “In the face of the rapidly intensifying climate crisis, climate adaptation is no longer a task that can be delayed, but a global imperative.” He added, “Through this training, we will share Korea’s outstanding policy experiences, further strengthen cooperation with Asia-Pacific countries, and make a tangible contribution to achieving the goals of the Paris Agreement.”

text:
▷ Ministry of Environment joins Sixth Forum of Ministers and Environment Authorities of Asia Pacific, reviews draft resolution for the 7th UNEA
The Ministry of Environment (Minister Kim Sungwhan) announced that from August 26 to 29, Jeong Eun-hae, Director General for International Cooperation Bureau at the Ministry of Environment, will attend the ‘Sixth Forum of Ministers and Environment Authorities of Asia Pacific’ (6th AP Forum) as the chief representative. The forum will be held in Nadi, a city located on the western side of Viti Levu, Fiji, in the South Pacific. Discussions will focus on strengthening cooperation to address regional environmental issues.
The 6th AP Forum is a regional preparatory meeting for the United Nations Environment Assembly (UNEA), which is held every two years in Nairobi, Kenya. Senior officials from 41 member countries in the Asia-Pacific region review the agenda of the upcoming UNEA at this forum to ensure that the policy priorities of the Asia-Pacific region are reflected.
The 6th AP Forum is being held to prepare for the 7th UNEA (UNEA-7), which is scheduled to take place in Nairobi this December. The 4th AP Forum was previously held in Suwon, South Korea, in October 2021.
Fiji, the host country of this forum, is the first among the Small Island Developing States (SIDS) in the Asia-Pacific region to host the AP Forum. Fiji has been at the forefront of the global response to the climate crisis, having hosted the 23rd Conference of the Parties (COP23) to the UN Climate Change Convention. This forum is expected to call for international cooperation to address challenges such as sea level rise and coral ecosystem degradation caused by the climate crisis.
Director General Jeong, who will attend the forum as the chief representative, plans to emphasize the importance of transitioning to a circular economy to address the three major crises: the climate crisis, biodiversity loss, and global pollution.
In particular, South Korea plans to build upon the Circular Economy Action Initiative announced at the World Environment Day commemoration event (June 5, Jeju) this year (2025) and present a draft resolution on promoting international environmental cooperation for advancing the circular economy.
The draft resolution affirms that a comprehensive and precise assessment is essential to address waste pollution problems, which arise from complex factors, in a country-specific manner; calls for the establishment of joint investigative teams composed of international organizations such as the UN Environment Programme, experts, civil society, and other stakeholders to effectively diagnose environmental challenges; and aims to contribute to practical international environmental cooperation for achieving a circular economy.
In addition, Director General Jeong will attend side events jointly organized by the Ministry of Environment and international organizations during the 6th AP Forum, where she will deliver opening and congratulatory remarks to emphasize the need for international cooperation in achieving a circular economy for electric vehicle waste batteries and in meeting air quality goals in the Asia-Pacific region.
Director General Jeong stated, “The Asia-Pacific region accounts for 60% of the world’s population and is a key area of environmental governance that will shape the direction of discussions at the next UNEA.” She added, “Based on our experience and capabilities, Korea will actively serve as a central medium of international cooperation to effectively promote the circular economy in Asia-Pacific countries.”

text:
▷ Expanding practical cooperation in climate change, including international greenhouse gas mitigation projects
The 3rd Korea-Malaysia Climate Change Dialogue to strengthen cooperation between Korea and Malaysia on responding to climate change was held on Monday, August 25, in Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia. The meeting was led by Chung Keeyong, Ambassador and Deputy Minister for Climate Change from Korea’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Datuk Nor Yahati binti Awang, Deputy Secretary General for Environmental Sustainability at Malaysia’s Ministry of Natural Resources and Environmental Sustainability, as chief delegates. Officials from related government ministries and agencies, including the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, the Ministry of Environment, the Sudokwon Landfill Site Management Corp., and the Korea Environment Corporation, also attended the meeting.
※ The Korea-Malaysia Climate Change Dialogue was newly established during the Korea-Malaysia Foreign Ministers’ Meeting in May 2023 to strengthen bilateral cooperation on climate change response. The first meeting was held in Malaysia in October 2023, and the second meeting was held in Korea in September 2024.
At this meeting, the two countries presented their domestic climate change policies aimed at achieving carbon neutrality by 2050 and exchanged views on the main negotiation trends related to the 30th UN Climate Change Conference of the Parties (COP30), to be held in November this year. Furthermore, they discussed the Basic Agreement on Bilateral Climate Change Cooperation and international mitigation projects* between the two countries utilizing Article 6.2 of the Paris Agreement.
* Reduction outcomes issued from international mitigation projects through voluntary cooperation between countries are utilized to achieve Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC).
The Korean side introduced the government’s climate change response policies, including Korea’s implementation of the NDC, the emissions trading system, and the national climate crisis adaptation plan. In addition, Korea’s environmental integrity standards for Article 6.2 projects under the Paris Agreement and the Korea-specific Readiness program designed to support greenhouse gas reduction in host countries of international mitigation projects were also presented.
Furthermore, the Korean side shared the current progress and future plans of two ongoing international greenhouse gas mitigation projects in Malaysia and expressed the hope to expand such projects in the field of waste management between Korea and Malaysia. At present, Korea is carrying out a project to produce bioenergy using Malaysia’s organic waste, such as palm oil sludge.
In addition, as a follow-up to the Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) signed last November for the implementation of greenhouse gas reduction projects, the two countries agreed to launch negotiations to conclude a bilateral climate change cooperation agreement. This is evaluated as having laid the foundation for expanding practical cooperation between the two countries in the field of international greenhouse gas mitigation.
Ambassador and Deputy Minister Chung stated, “Through the 3rd Korea-Malaysia Climate Change Dialogue, we reaffirmed the strong complementarity of our mutual interests and the great potential for win-win cooperation in responding to climate change, and created a meaningful turning point to deepen coordination in international climate negotiations.” The two countries agreed to hold the fourth meeting in Seoul next year.

▷ The 11th Tripartite Policy Dialogue on Biodiversity to be held in Jeju, August 26-27
▷ Six agenda items to be discussed, including implementation of National Biodiversity Strategy and Action Plan and response to natural capital disclosure
The Ministry of Environment (Minister Kim Sungwhan) announced that it will hold the ‘11th Tripartite Policy Dialogue on Biodiversity’ (“Policy Dialogue”) at the Haevichi Hotel & Resort in Seogwipo, Jeju, for two days starting August 26, to promote exchanges on biodiversity conservation policies among Korea, China, and Japan.
The Policy Dialogue is an intergovernmental meeting in the field of biodiversity, proposed by Korea at the 14th Tripartite Environment Ministers Meeting (TEMM*) in 2012. Director-level officials from each country participate, and since 2013, the three countries have taken turns hosting it annually.
* The Tripartite Environment Ministers Meeting (TEMM) is a conference where the environment ministers of Korea, China, and Japan gather to discuss environmental issues in Northeast Asia, such as pollution and ecosystem destruction, and to promote sustainable development. It has been held annually since 1999.
The 11th Policy Dialogue will be hosted by Korea, with the participation of around 30 officials in charge of biodiversity from Korea, China, and Japan, as well as related experts.
The six main agenda items are: implementation of National Biodiversity Strategy and Action Plan, identification of subsidies affecting biodiversity, benefit-sharing of genetic resources, expanding private-sector participation in biodiversity conservation such as natural capital disclosure, management of invasive alien species, and other biodiversity issues of each country.
The National Biodiversity Strategy and Action Plan was established by each country to reflect the ‘Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework (GBF),’ a global biodiversity strategy adopted at the Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD) Conference in December 2022. In this Policy Dialogue, Korea, China, and Japan will share the main contents and implementation status of their respective national strategies and seek ways to cooperate toward achieving the goals.
In addition, discussions will be held on policy measures to increase private-sector participation in biodiversity conservation, such as natural capital disclosure, which requires companies to analyze and disclose the impacts of their activities on biodiversity.
Kim Tae-oh, Director General of Nature Conservation Bureau at the Ministry of Environment, stated, “By February next year, each country must submit an implementation report on its National Biodiversity Strategy and Action Plan to the international community.” He added, “Through this Policy Dialogue, we will share the implementation status of each country’s biodiversity strategies, discuss various issues, and seek ways to strengthen cooperation for the advancement of biodiversity policies among the three countries.”

▷ Exploring cooperation measures for water security and climate crisis response, including AI flood forecasting, low-carbon hydrogen production strategies, and removal of radioactive materials in seawater desalination
▷ Discussing ways to expand water leakage reduction projects in the UAE
The Ministry of Environment (Minister Kim Sungwhan) announced that it will hold the 8th Korea-United Arab Emirates (UAE) Joint Committee on Water Resources Cooperation at the Han River Flood Control Office (located in Seocho-gu, Seoul) on August 27.
In February 2024, the UAE, under the leadership of the President, launched the “Mohamed bin Zayed Water Initiative” to address the global water shortage crisis, devoting national capacity to developing innovative and sustainable water management solutions and strengthening international cooperation. In April of the same year, record rainfall caused damage in the Dubai area, prompting the country to pursue large-scale flood control projects, showing its strong interest in water management technologies. In addition, since a significant portion of its drinking water is obtained through seawater desalination, the UAE is also highly focused on securing water security against potential incidents of radioactive material inflow into seawater.
In November 2015, the two countries signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) on water resources cooperation and have since been strengthening collaboration in areas such as surface water, groundwater, smart water management, and seawater desalination. Since 2017, the Joint Committee on Water Resources Cooperation has been held alternately in both countries every year, and in November of last year, the 7th Joint Committee was held virtually.
In 2022, a domestic research team established a demonstration facility in the Middle East with the goal of developing low-energy seawater desalination technology, and since last year, a pilot project* to reduce water leakage rates in the UAE has been underway.
* In the Dibba region of the UAE, the project aims to improve the water flow rate by 10 percentage points over a 10 km pipeline section (from 62% to 72%).
At the 8th Joint Committee, Korea will be represented by Kim Hyo-jung, Director General of Water Use Policy Bureau at the Ministry of Environment, along with domestic water management experts. The UAE will be represented by Sharif Al Olama, Undersecretary of the Ministry of Energy & Infrastructure, accompanied by officials from Etihad and Dubai Electricity and Water Authority.
At the Joint Committee, discussions will include strengthening disaster response with AI-based flood forecasting, low-carbon hydrogen production strategies, digital twin-based water management, tritium removal in seawater desalination, modernization and reuse of wastewater treatment plants, as well as pilot projects with smart water network management and promotion of joint research.
In addition, concrete plans will be made for various cooperation measures, including a joint side event at the UN Water Conference* to be held in the UAE in December 2026, as well as the coordination of the 9th Joint Committee.
* A high-level international water conference hosted by the UN, aimed at accelerating the resolution of water issues through international cooperation
Director General Kim Hyo-jung stated, “This Joint Committee is an opportunity to solidify cooperation between the two countries, focusing on Korea’s AI-based flood forecasting and digital twin technologies, and the UAE’s efforts to secure low-carbon hydrogen energy.” She added, “While strengthening both countries’ responses to the climate crisis, we plan to identify and advance cooperation measures that will enable Korean water companies to play an active role.”

title: Press Release
text:
▷ Holding cooperation seminars and export consultations to connect local demand with Korean companies
▷ Signing MOUs for demonstration projects and carrying them out based on past cooperation 
The Ministry of Environment (Minister Kim Sunghwan) and the Ministry of Foreign Affairs (Minister Cho Hyun) will dispatch a ‘Korea-Kazakhstan Water Industry Cooperation Delegation*’ to Kazakhstan from September 1 to 5 to support the entry of domestic water industry companies into Central Asia and to strengthen cooperation in the water sector.
* Ministry of Environment, Ministry of Foreign Affairs, K-water, Korea Environment Corporation (National Water Industry Cluster), Korea Water Partnership, Korea Trade-Investment Promotion Agency, 13 domestic water companies
Kazakhstan, as a downstream country of transboundary rivers in Central Asia, relies heavily on external sources for water, with about 45% of its water resources flowing in from neighboring countries, which drives strong interest in sustainable water management technologies. In addition, in response to aging water supply and sewage facilities, the country is actively expanding investment in water management infrastructure and introducing digital and smart water technologies, making it a nation considered to have high potential for cooperation in the water industry.
In addition, Kazakhstan has shown strong interest in Korea’s advanced water industry technologies and a willingness to cooperate. Since 2019, the two sides have continuously engaged in cooperation* through the dispatch of water industry cooperation delegations and holding consultations. In 2021, during the Kazakh president’s visit to Korea, the two countries signed a memorandum of understanding on water resources cooperation.
* 2019: First dispatch of water industry cooperation delegation; 2020-2022: Consultations and online business meetings; 2023-present: Consecutive delegation dispatches
On September 3, the delegation will hold the Korea-Kazakhstan Water Industry Cooperation Seminar, institutional meetings, and a business consultation session for water companies. These events will share the current status and key technologies of the water industry in both countries, introduce support systems for overseas expansion of water companies, and facilitate one-on-one consultations between companies by sector.
At the cooperation seminar, the governments and related institutions of both countries will share key water management policies and cooperative projects, while domestic water companies will present their advanced technologies. This will be followed by meetings with major Kazakh government ministries and related organizations to discuss upcoming projects and explore potential areas of cooperation.
※(Participating institutions from Kazakhstan) Ministry of Water Resources and Irrigation, Ministry of Industry and Construction, Committee on Water Resources, Committee for the Regulation, Protection and Use of Water Resources, Center for Modernization and Development of Housing and Communal Services, Kazvodkhoz, Astana Waterworks, Almaty Waterworks, etc.
At the water industry business consultation session, Korean companies - selected based on prior market assessments and demand surveys conducted through KOTRA Almaty - will meet with Kazakh companies for one-on-one consultations in areas of mutual interest such as water treatment technologies and wastewater treatment systems.
In addition, building on past cooperation, during the delegation’s visit, mutual cooperation MOUs will be signed with the waterworks authorities of Astana and Almaty to promote joint projects and technology demonstrations. Pilot projects will also be carried out for water treatment facilities and flow meters.
Kim Hyo-jung, Director General of Water Use Policy Bureau at the Ministry of Environment, stated, “As a result of our continued support for the entry of Korean water companies into Kazakhstan, we are now seeing tangible outcomes such as supply contracts and demonstration projects.” She added, “We will continue working to connect local demand with the excellent technologies and products of our companies.”
Han Min-young, Director-General for Climate Change, Energy, Environment and Scientific Affairs Bureau at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, said, “Kazakhstan is an important partner in Central Asia, and we expect that this delegation will substantially strengthen the foundation for Korean water companies to enter the Kazakh market.” She added, “We will work to create an environment that enables our companies to expand into overseas water markets and strive to spread outcomes of sustainable growth and mutual prosperity.”
The Ministry of Environment and the Ministry of Foreign Affairs plan to continue working closely together to ensure that the outcomes of this delegation lead to tangible results, such as export contracts for Korea’s advanced water management technologies and high-quality products.

text:
▷ Intergovernmental cooperation on climate change and waste management, and support for overseas expansion of domestic companies
The Ministry of Environment (Minister Kim Sunghwan) announced that it will dispatch a “Green Industry Environmental Cooperation Mission” to Accra, the capital of Ghana, from September 2 to 3.
This dispatch is aimed at discussing cooperation measures for urgent environmental issues in Ghana and neighboring countries, and establishing a cooperation network with the local government.
Although Africa has the lowest carbon emissions among all continents, it is highly vulnerable to the impacts of climate change, such as rising temperatures, decreased rainfall leading to reduced agricultural productivity, and urbanization, which pose serious threats to its socio-economic development.
Accordingly, since the early 2000s, the Ministry of Environment has steadily promoted environmental cooperation with Africa. Currently, it is carrying out projects such as establishing a smart water management system for the Accra water supply in Ghana (2023-2026, grant aid) and installing landfill gas incineration and power generation facilities at the Adipa landfill site (pre-feasibility study underway, 2024-2025).
The environmental cooperation mission to be dispatched this time plans to promote collaboration in green industry fields such as waste management, landfill gas power generation, and carbon reduction and adaptation through: intergovernmental environmental cooperation meetings with Ghanaian government agencies (Ministry of Local Government, Chieftaincy, and Religious Affairs [MLGCR], Ministry of Environment, Science and Technology [MEST]), the Korea-Africa Environmental Cooperation Forum, and business consultations between domestic climate and waste management companies and government officials from six African countries*.
* Ghana, Senegal, Egypt, Uganda, Tanzania, Cote d’Ivoire
On the first day (September 2), the Korea-Africa Environmental Cooperation Forum will be held to share and discuss the impacts of climate change in Africa, resilience and adaptation measures, climate-related policies and technologies of each country, and approaches to investment.
On the second day (September 3), the Ministry of Environment, the Ghanaian government, and international organizations will hold a cooperation meeting to discuss mutual support for planned projects in the climate and waste sectors, as well as the development of follow-up projects. In addition, business consultations will be conducted between Korean companies and six African countries, including Ghana.
In particular, Ghana, which has jointly developed and promoted bilateral international carbon reduction projects with Switzerland and issued international reduction credits in July this year, is one of the countries actively advancing climate-related initiatives. It is expected to serve as a strategic hub for Korean companies entering the African market in the field of climate change projects.
Jung Eun-hae, Director General of the International Cooperation Bureau at the Ministry of Environment, stated, “Through this dispatch to Ghana, we will identify environmental issues across the African continent, including Ghana, and introduce Korea’s cutting-edge environmental technologies and industries to create an opportunity to strengthen cooperation.” She added, “We will serve as a stepping stone for Korean companies seeking to enter the African market.”

text:
▷ Co-hosted by the Ministry of Environment and the Global Environment Facility (GEF), with participation from 85 countries, international organizations, and multilateral development banks
▷ Sharing outcomes and lessons from Biennial Transparency Reports (BTR), discussing the 2035 Nationally Determined Contributions (NDC)
The Ministry of Environment (Minister Kim Sunghwan) announced that it will hold the 2nd Global Transparency Forum* jointly with the Global Environment Facility (GEF) from September 3 to 5 at Songdo Convensia (located in Yeonsu-gu, Incheon).
* In accordance with Article 13 of the Paris Agreement, the Global Environment Facility is promoting this international event to support developing countries in preparing Biennial Transparency Reports and monitoring their greenhouse gas reduction activities. The 1st Forum (2024) was hosted by Japan (Ministry of the Environment).
This event has been organized to effectively implement the Enhanced Transparency Framework under Article 13 of the Paris Agreement. More than 150 participants, including government officials from 85 developing countries, major international organizations, and representatives of multilateral development banks, will attend.
The event, under the theme “Transparency for Transformation: Strengthening Systems, Driving Ambition.” will provide a platform for countries to share the experiences and lessons learned from preparing their first Biennial Transparency Reports.
Transparency is a key tool for objectively evaluating greenhouse gas reduction performance and building international trust. The Biennial Transparency Report is used to assess whether countries are implementing their submitted Nationally Determined Contributions and serves as a basis for verifying reductions generated in international carbon markets.
This event serves as an international forum to link transparency reporting and review directly to policy, investment, and cooperation.
On the first day of the event, September 3, a high-level dialogue will be held with representatives from both developing and developed countries. At this session, Jeong Eun-hae, Director General for International Cooperation Bureau at the Ministry of Environment, will represent the Korean government as a panelist, sharing Korea’s experience with transparency systems and emphasizing the importance of strengthening cooperation and action within the international community.
The Greenhouse Gas Inventory and Research Center of Korea, under the Ministry of Environment, will give a presentation on the achievements and challenges encountered during Korea’s preparation of the Biennial Transparency Report, as well as future plans for institutional improvements.
On the second day, discussions will focus on linking policies and investments in relation to the design of the 2035 Nationally Determined Contribution, as well as the use of climate finance and examples of international cooperation. On the same day, a “Transparency Bazaar” will be held, where government officials and representatives from international organizations will explore ways to connect programs, funding, and technology for cooperation.
On the final day, countries including Korea will present cases of institutionalizing transparency, with the aim of identifying best practices that can be applied to other nations. Following this, international organizations such as the GEF will introduce global programs and future resource utilization plans to strengthen transparency capacity in developing countries.
Jeong Eun-hae, Director General for International Cooperation Bureau, stated, “Transparency goes beyond a mere reporting obligation; it is a fundamental basis for building trust among nations and accelerating climate action.” She added, “I hope this event will serve as a starting point for sharing experiences and challenges among countries, and for fostering new cooperation and investment.”
